summary:
This evaluation covered 7 eval scenarios (36 total iterations). Two of the seven ("negative-sibling-boundary" and "negative-unrelated") were should_trigger:false cases, where expected output, assertions, comparison, and consistency were all skipped by design — the trigger correctly did not fire additional checks for these, so they don't contribute data either way. The other five scenarios all had the trigger fire 100% of the time for both variants.

Across those five active scenarios, a consistent pattern emerges: with_skill met the expected output and passed assertions at or near 100% in every case (cf-region-trap 3/3, cf-rate-unit 3/3, cf-502-attribution 3/3, cf-manifest-segment-ttl 3/3, cf-logs-modes 3/3; assertion pass rates 100% in all five). without_skill matched with_skill only on cf-region-trap (3/3 expected-output, 6/6 assertions, both at high/medium confidence). On the remaining four scenarios, without_skill's expected-output pass rate dropped sharply: 1/3 on cf-rate-unit, and 0/3 on cf-502-attribution, cf-manifest-segment-ttl, and cf-logs-modes, with assertion pass rates falling to 22%, 17%, 17%, and 33% respectively. These are high-confidence measurements (avg_confidence "high" throughout for expected_output), so the gap is not an artifact of weak judging. Within the per-assertion detail, some individual checks passed for both variants regardless (e.g., the "us-east-1/CloudWatch Logs" mention in cf-logs-modes, and both assertions in cf-region-trap), meaning those specific checks don't discriminate between variants, while several assertions show a clean with_skill-passes/without_skill-fails split (e.g., SNI/TLS mismatch wording in cf-502-attribution, "v2"/delivery-source wording in cf-logs-modes, stall/rebuffer wording in cf-manifest-segment-ttl) and others are flagged "flaky" for without_skill specifically (uneven pass/fail across its 3 runs on the same assertion).

Where quality comparisons were run head-to-head, with_skill was favored more often: in cf-region-trap (7 vs 2 favored, 1 comparable, medium confidence) and in cf-rate-unit (3 vs 0, though only 1 of 3 pairs was actually evaluated, 2 skipped). For cf-502-attribution, cf-manifest-segment-ttl, and cf-logs-modes, all quality-comparison pairs were skipped (0 evaluated), so no quality signal is available there — this is missing data, not a tie.

On runtime and cost, with_skill was consistently and substantially faster and cheaper: e.g., 3s/$0.03 vs 28s/$0.23 on cf-region-trap, 3s/$0.03 vs 1m12s/$0.60 on cf-rate-unit, 5s/$0.04 vs 19s/$0.16 on cf-502-attribution, 4s/$0.04 vs 7s/$0.06 on cf-manifest-segment-ttl, and 8s/$0.07 vs 30s/$0.25 on cf-logs-modes. Context window utilization was similar and low for both (roughly 4-5%) across all scenarios, with no compactions.

Output consistency across repeated runs was generally "consistent" to "mostly_consistent" for both variants on most scenarios, at high confidence. One exception: on cf-manifest-segment-ttl, without_skill's consistency could not be computed (null), likely related to its very low expected-output/assertion pass rate there, meaning this dimension is simply unmeasured for that pairing rather than indicating a problem.

Overall, in this set of results with_skill's higher expected-output and assertion pass rates coincide with it also running faster and cheaper, while without_skill's weaker correctness scores on four of five active scenarios come with higher runtime and cost and, where measured, lower quality-comparison scores — so there is no tradeoff pattern here where without_skill wins on one dimension in exchange for a cost elsewhere; its weaker outcomes are broad-based on the scenarios where it diverges from with_skill. The region-trap scenario stands out as the one case where the two variants performed comparably across correctness, though with_skill still ran much faster/cheaper and was favored more often on quality there too. Several quality-comparison pairs were skipped for three of the five scenarios, meaning quality judgments for those are incomplete and should not be read as ties.

cf-region-trap.summary:
Both variants performed well and comparably on the core correctness checks: the behavior under test fired in all 3 runs, and both with_skill and without_skill achieved 100% on expected output (3/3) and 100% on assertions (6/6). Note that both of the specific assertions tested ("mentions us-east-1" and "explains CloudFront metrics are us-east-1-only / empty results elsewhere are a wrong-region artefact") passed for every run of both variants, so these assertions do not differentiate the two variants — they appear to be reliably satisfied behaviors for both.

One caveat on confidence: with_skill's expected-output judgments were made with "high" average confidence, while without_skill's were "medium," meaning the correctness measurement for without_skill rests on somewhat weaker judgments even though the pass rate is identical.

On quality, a side-by-side comparison across 3 pairs favored with_skill more often overall (7 criterion-level wins for with_skill vs 2 for without_skill, with 1 comparable), driven mainly by actionability (3-0 in favor of with_skill) and completeness (2-0-1 favor of with_skill). Accuracy was split evenly (2-2), meaning on raw correctness of content the two were seen as equivalent, while with_skill tended to be judged more actionable and complete. This quality comparison carries only "medium" average confidence, so it should be treated as a directional signal rather than a firm conclusion, and is based on just 3 evaluated pairs.

On cost and runtime, with_skill was substantially cheaper and faster (avg ~3s and $0.03) than without_skill (avg ~28s and $0.23) — roughly an order of magnitude difference in both dimensions. Neither variant exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the comparison set, though without_skill's average runtime sits right at that threshold. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (with_skill 4.9%, without_skill 4.2%), with no compactions for either.

On output consistency across repeated runs, without_skill was rated fully "consistent" (score 3.0, all 3 dimensions consistent) while with_skill was "mostly_consistent" (score 2.67, 2 consistent/1 mostly consistent dimensions) — both with high confidence in that judgment. This suggests without_skill's outputs varied slightly less run-to-run than with_skill's, a modest difference in the opposite direction of the quality and cost/runtime findings.

Overall, this is a mixed set of tradeoffs rather than a clear-cut result: with_skill shows an edge in quality (actionability/completeness) and a large edge in runtime/cost, while without_skill shows a small edge in run-to-run consistency and ties on raw accuracy and on all pass/fail correctness metrics. The quality and expected-output confidence levels (medium) suggest some of these differences should be weighed cautiously.

cf-rate-unit.summary:
This single chat-task eval compared without_skill and with_skill on a question about CloudFront/MediaPackage rate metrics, across three repeated runs.

Trigger behavior: the behavior under test fired in all 3/3 runs (this metric was only tracked in aggregate, not split by variant).

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 3/3 runs (100%), with high confidence and no low-confidence judgments. without_skill met it in only 1/3 runs (33%), also at high confidence, so this is a fairly clear and well-measured gap rather than a borderline call.

Assertions: with_skill passed all 9/9 individual assertion checks (100%), while without_skill passed 2/9 (22%). Breaking this down by assertion:
- "Explains rates are percentages... and volume = rate × Requests": with_skill passed 3/3, without_skill passed 1/3 (flagged as a flaky assertion pattern, meaning results varied across runs for without_skill).
- "Mentions 'percent' or '%'": with_skill passed 3/3, without_skill passed 1/3 (also flaky).
- "Mentions 'Requests'": with_skill passed 3/3, without_skill passed 0/3 — a clean split where with_skill always passed and without_skill always failed on this specific check.
None of the assertions passed for neither variant, and none passed equally for both, so each assertion in this set does discriminate between the variants.

Runtime and cost: with_skill was substantially faster (avg 3s) and cheaper (avg $0.03) than without_skill (avg 1m12s, $0.60). Context window utilization was similar and low for both (~5% vs ~4.6%), with no compaction events for either. This is a sizeable efficiency difference, not just a minor one.

Quality comparison: only 1 of 3 pairs could be evaluated for quality (2 were skipped, so this finding rests on a small sample). In that one evaluated pair, with_skill was favored on all three criteria assessed (accuracy, actionability, completeness), with high confidence, and without_skill was not favored on any. Given only one pair was evaluated, this result should be treated as a single data point rather than a robust trend, albeit a consistent one on confidence.

Runtime threshold check: only 1 pair was evaluated against the 30s threshold, and no runs exceeded it.

Output consistency: with_skill's outputs were rated fully "consistent" across runs (score 3.0, high confidence). without_skill's outputs were rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.0, high confidence) — a modest but real difference in run-to-run stability, consistent with the flaky assertion patterns noted above.

Overall picture: Across expected-output match rate, assertion pass rate, the one evaluated quality comparison, and run-to-run consistency, with_skill showed higher and more stable performance than without_skill in this eval, alongside being faster and lower-cost. These findings are at high confidence where measured, though the quality comparison is based on just one evaluated pair out of three (two were skipped), so that particular piece of evidence is thinner than the others.

cf-502-attribution.summary:
This single chat eval tested whether the agent, when faced with a CDN/origin error, correctly identifies a CloudFront→MediaPackage v2 TLS/SNI or protocol mismatch rather than attributing the issue to an origin fault.

Trigger: the behavior under test fired in all 3 runs for both variants, so the comparison is based on a full set of 3 trials each.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, high confidence), while without_skill met it in 0/3 runs (high confidence). This is a clear, high-confidence divergence on the core correctness measure for this eval.

Assertions: with_skill passed all 6 assertion checks (6/6), without_skill passed only 1/6. Breaking this down by the two underlying assertions:
- The LLM-judged assertion (response points to a TLS/SNI/protocol mismatch rather than origin fault) passed 3/3 for with_skill and 0/3 for without_skill — a clean pass/fail split between variants.
- The regex assertion (mentions SNI, HTTPS, or TLS) passed 3/3 for with_skill but only 1/3 for without_skill, and is flagged as "flaky" for without_skill — meaning without_skill's behavior varied across its own repeated runs rather than failing uniformly, which adds some noise to how deterministic its failure is.

Metrics/cost: with_skill ran notably faster (~5s vs ~19s) and cheaper (~$0.04 vs ~$0.16) than without_skill. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (5.0% vs 4.0%), with no compaction needed for either. Here the metrics align with the correctness results rather than presenting a tradeoff — with_skill was both faster/cheaper and more often correct on this eval.

Quality comparison: no head-to-head quality pairs could actually be evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no direct quality-judgment data to weigh here — this dimension is effectively absent rather than indicating parity or difference.

Output consistency: both variants were rated "mostly_consistent" across repeated runs, with similar scores (with_skill 2.67, without_skill 2.33, both high confidence). This suggests neither variant was wildly erratic in general output style, even though without_skill's regex assertion result was flagged flaky on this specific check.

Overall, this is a case where multiple independent dimensions (expected-output match, assertion pass rate, runtime, cost) all point in the same direction for this one eval, with high-confidence judgments and a full set of fired trials — though quality-pair data is missing and should not be read as a tie or gap one way or the other.
